title: Climate and disaster risk can move homeowner losses into household and federal exposure
source_unit: Congressional Budget Office policy analysis, Climate Change, Disaster Risk, and Homeowner's Insurance, August 2024
geography: United States; national policy and modeled federal exposure frame

observations.period: 2023; natural-disaster loss and insurance coverage aggregate
observations.method: CBO policy analysis citing national natural-disaster loss and insurance coverage aggregates; this is not a household panel or claims file.
observations.uncertainty: The aggregate does not identify peril, geography, policy terms, deductibles, public aid, underinsurance, recovery time, or the distribution of the uncovered loss across households and governments.
observations.subgroup: Natural-disaster losses and insurers at the national level; CBO separately notes greater uninsured or underinsured exposure and slower recovery among lower- and moderate-income households.
observations.counterinterpretation: An uninsured share of loss is not the same as an uninsured household: deductibles, exclusions, limits, self-insurance, public assistance, and other coverage can all contribute.

observations.period: 2024 report; federally guaranteed mortgage and mortgage-security exposure

denominator.unit: trillion dollars of federally guaranteed mortgages and mortgage securities

observations.method: CBO policy analysis of the federal role in housing finance and disaster exposure.
observations.uncertainty: This is the scale of a federally connected mortgage and securities exposure, not a forecast of loss and not a measure of currently uninsured borrowers or homes.
observations.subgroup: Borrowers, lenders, mortgage guarantors, mortgage securities, and federal institutions connected to federally backed housing finance.
observations.counterinterpretation: Federal backing can distribute and reduce some private financing risk without guaranteeing adequate insurance, fast repair, or household recovery after a disaster.

observations.period: CBO model comparison; 2020 climate conditions versus 2050 climate conditions

denominator.unit: year expected flood-damage modeling horizon for homes with federally backed mortgages

modeled_increase.unit: billion dollars between the report's climate-condition scenarios

observations.method: CBO model comparison for expected flood damage to homes with federally backed mortgages under different climate conditions.
observations.uncertainty: The comparison is scenario-dependent and does not predict realized claims, premiums, relocation, public aid, or the timing of damage. The difference should not be read as a causal estimate of any one policy.
observations.subgroup: Homes with federally backed mortgages in the modeled flood-exposure frame.
observations.counterinterpretation: Mitigation, adaptation, rebuilding standards, insurance changes, migration, and mortgage-market composition can change realized losses relative to a static scenario comparison.

observations.period: 2024 report; lower- and moderate-income recovery mechanism

denominator.unit: CBO policy-analysis finding about household income groups

observations.method: CBO synthesis of insurance, disaster, and household-recovery evidence; no single same-household causal estimate is asserted here.
observations.uncertainty: The report-level comparison does not identify how much of the recovery difference comes from insurance, wealth, housing quality, location, labor disruption, public aid, or other resources.
observations.subgroup: Lower- and moderate-income households compared with higher-income households after disaster loss.
observations.counterinterpretation: Income can be correlated with many forms of exposure and recovery capacity; the finding should not be converted into an income-only causal claim.

related_sources.claim: FHFA supplies home-price index data for separating modeled insurance exposure from observed housing-price movements.
Treasury's Federal Insurance Office supplies a federal insurance-policy and market context layer.
Federal Reserve SHED supplies household-level insurance status and affordability evidence to pair with CBO's policy and modeled layer.

boundary: This record adds a national policy-analysis and modeled federal-exposure layer. It does not establish that climate risk caused a particular household's premium, nonrenewal, mortgage trouble, repair delay, sale, move, or political response. Those links require property- and household-level records with compatible dates and denominators.
